name: War of the Pacific
summary: Chile fought Bolivia and Peru over the nitrate-rich Atacama coast after Bolivia raised taxes on a Chilean nitrate company. Chile won control of the sea, took the southern deserts and occupied Lima, then beat down a long guerrilla resistance in the Andes. Peru lost Tarapaca and Bolivia lost its whole coastline, leaving it landlocked to this day.

steps.label: Feb 1879
steps.title: Seizure of Antofagasta
steps.text: Bolivia raised a tax on the Chilean nitrate company in Antofagasta and moved to seize its property. Chilean troops landed and took the port without a fight on 14 February 1879. Peru was bound to Bolivia by a secret alliance, so Chile declared war on both in April.

events.name: Occupation of Antofagasta
events.text: Chilean troops occupy the Bolivian port, starting the war.

steps.label: May to Oct 1879
steps.title: War at sea
steps.text: Neither side could march an army across the Atacama, so the war began as a fight for the sea. Arturo Prat died aboard the Esmeralda at Iquique, but Peru lost its ironclad Independencia the same day. Miguel Grau's Huascar raided the Chilean coast for months until it was trapped and captured off Punta Angamos, giving Chile command of the sea.

events.name: Battle of Iquique
events.text: Prat's Esmeralda is sunk, but Peru loses the Independencia at nearby Punta Gruesa.

events.name: Battle of Angamos
events.text: The Huascar is captured and Grau killed; Chile now controls the coast.

steps.label: Nov 1879
steps.title: Tarapaca campaign
steps.text: With the sea secure, Chile landed an army at Pisagua and beat the allies at San Francisco (Dolores). Bolivian President Daza marched from Tacna to help but turned back at Camarones. The allies won a rearguard fight at Tarapaca yet had to abandon the nitrate province and fall back on Arica and Tacna.

events.name: Landing at Pisagua
events.text: Chilean troops storm ashore and open the way into Tarapaca.

events.name: Battle of San Francisco
events.text: The allied army breaks and Iquique falls.

events.name: Battle of Tarapaca
events.text: Peruvians win the fight but must still retreat north.

steps.label: May to Jun 1880
steps.title: Tacna and Arica
steps.text: General Manuel Baquedano landed at Ilo and marched on Tacna, where he routed the combined Peruvian and Bolivian army. Bolivia effectively left the war. Days later Chilean infantry stormed the headland of Arica, where Colonel Francisco Bolognesi died refusing to surrender.

events.name: Battle of Tacna
events.text: The allied army is destroyed at the Alto de la Alianza.

events.name: Battle of Arica
events.text: The Morro of Arica is stormed in under an hour.

steps.label: Jan 1881
steps.title: Fall of Lima
steps.text: Chile shipped about 26,000 men north, landing at Pisco and Lurin. Baquedano broke Pierola's defence lines at Chorrillos and Miraflores in January 1881 and occupied Lima. Pierola fled to the highlands and Peru had no national government that would accept Chile's terms.

events.name: Battle of Chorrillos
events.text: The first Peruvian line falls after heavy fighting.

events.name: Battle of Miraflores
events.text: The last defence of Lima collapses; Chile enters the capital.

steps.label: 1882 to 1883
steps.title: Campaign of the Brena
steps.text: From the Andes, Andres Avelino Caceres led a guerrilla war of soldiers and highland villagers against the occupation. His men wiped out a Chilean garrison at Concepcion in July 1882. A year later Colonel Alejandro Gorostiaga caught and crushed Caceres's army at Huamachuco, ending organised resistance.

fronts.label: Occupied coast vs Andean resistance, c. 1882

events.name: Battle of Concepcion
events.text: A Chilean company is annihilated by Caceres's forces.

events.name: Battle of Huamachuco
events.text: Caceres's army is destroyed, ending large-scale resistance.

steps.label: 1883 to 1884
steps.title: Ancon and Valparaiso
steps.text: Peru signed the Treaty of Ancon in October 1883, ceding Tarapaca and leaving Tacna and Arica under Chilean control. Chilean troops then left Lima. Bolivia signed a truce at Valparaiso in April 1884 that handed its coastal province to Chile and cut it off from the sea.

events.name: Treaty of Ancon
events.text: Peru cedes Tarapaca; Tacna and Arica pass to Chilean rule.

events.name: Truce of Valparaiso
events.text: Bolivia loses its Litoral province and becomes landlocked.

name: Anglo-Zulu War
summary: Britain invaded the Zulu kingdom in 1879 to force it into a South African confederation under British control. The Zulu army destroyed a British column at Isandlwana, one of the worst colonial defeats of the era, but British reinforcements and firepower won at Ulundi six months later. King Cetshwayo was captured and his kingdom broken into 13 chiefdoms.

steps.label: Jan 1879
steps.title: Invasion
steps.text: High Commissioner Bartle Frere sent Cetshwayo an ultimatum he could not accept, including disbanding the Zulu army. When it expired, Lord Chelmsford invaded with three columns: Pearson along the coast, the centre column at Rorke's Drift and Evelyn Wood in the north. Cetshwayo gathered his regiments at Ulundi.

events.name: British ultimatum expires
events.text: The ultimatum expires on 11 January and the columns cross into Zululand.

steps.label: 22 Jan 1879
steps.title: Isandlwana
steps.text: While Chelmsford split his force to chase a decoy, about 20,000 Zulu warriors under Ntshingwayo overran his camp at Isandlwana, killing some 1,300 men. That night a Zulu reserve under Dabulamanzi failed to take the small post at Rorke's Drift. On the coast, Pearson won at Nyezane but was then besieged at Eshowe.

events.name: Battle of Isandlwana
events.text: The Zulu army destroys the British centre column's camp.

events.name: Defence of Rorke's Drift
events.text: About 150 defenders hold the mission station overnight.

events.name: Siege of Eshowe
events.text: Pearson's column is cut off at Eshowe until April.

steps.label: Mar to Apr 1879
steps.title: Kambula and Eshowe
steps.text: Reinforcements poured into Natal. In the north, Wood's raid on Hlobane was beaten back, but the next day the main Zulu army broke itself against his fortified camp at Kambula. On the coast Chelmsford beat the Zulu at Gingindlovu and relieved Eshowe, and the war turned against Cetshwayo.

events.name: Battle of Hlobane
events.text: Wood's mounted troops are driven off the mountain.

events.name: Battle of Kambula
events.text: The decisive defeat of the Zulu army in the north.

events.name: Battle of Gingindlovu
events.text: Chelmsford's square repulses the Zulu and Eshowe is relieved.

steps.label: Jun to Jul 1879
steps.title: Ulundi
steps.text: Chelmsford invaded again with a much larger army, the 2nd Division and Wood's column marching on the royal kraal while the 1st Division moved up the coast. On 4 July his infantry formed a great square on the plain at Ulundi; the Zulu charges failed against rifles, artillery and Gatlings. The royal homestead was burned.

events.name: Battle of Ulundi
events.text: The Zulu army is defeated and oNdini is burned.

steps.label: Aug to Sep 1879
steps.title: Capture and partition
steps.text: Cetshwayo fled north and was captured in the Ngome forest on 28 August. Garnet Wolseley, who had replaced Chelmsford, split Zululand among 13 appointed chiefs, a settlement that led to civil war. Britain annexed what was left in 1887.

events.name: Capture of Cetshwayo
events.text: The king is taken in the Ngome forest and sent into exile.

events.name: Wolseley settlement
events.text: Zululand is divided into 13 chiefdoms under British oversight.

name: Conquest of the Desert
summary: Argentina's army, led by Julio Argentino Roca, pushed the frontier from the Buenos Aires pampas to the Rio Negro and then into the Andes and Patagonia. Armed with Remington rifles and the telegraph, it broke the Mapuche, Ranquel and Tehuelche chiefdoms; thousands were killed and some 14,000 captured and deported. The campaign doubled Argentina's effective territory and opened the south to ranching and immigration.

sides.name: Indigenous peoples of the Pampas and Patagonia

steps.label: 1876 to 1878
steps.title: Alsina's ditch
steps.text: Under Adolfo Alsina the army had dug a long ditch and line of forts across the pampas to stop raids on frontier ranches. After Alsina's death, War Minister Julio Argentino Roca argued for a full offensive. In 1878 raids broke the Salinero and Ranquel camps and captured the chief Pincen, and Congress funded an advance to the Rio Negro.

polities: Patagonian shellfish and marine mammal hunters

events.name: Law 947
events.text: Congress approves funds to push the frontier to the Rio Negro.

steps.label: Apr to Jun 1879
steps.title: March to the Rio Negro
steps.text: In April 1879 about 6,000 soldiers advanced in five divisions converging on the Rio Negro. Roca's own column marched from Azul via Carhue and reached Choele Choel on 25 May, while Uriburu's division came down from Mendoza to the Neuquen confluence. The riverline became the new frontier, cutting the pampas off from Patagonia.

polities: Patagonian shellfish and marine mammal hunters

events.name: Roca reaches Choele Choel
events.text: The army reaches the Rio Negro on 25 May, Argentina's national day.

steps.label: 1881 to 1883
steps.title: Into the Andes
steps.text: Conrado Villegas led columns up the Limay to Lake Nahuel Huapi in 1881 and swept Neuquen in the 1882 to 1883 Andes campaign. At the same time Chile was occupying Araucania across the mountains, so Mapuche communities were squeezed from both sides. The 1881 boundary treaty split Patagonia between the two states along the Andes.

events.name: Villegas reaches Nahuel Huapi
events.text: Argentine troops reach the great Andean lake.

events.name: Boundary Treaty of 1881
events.text: Argentina and Chile divide Patagonia along the Andes watershed.

events.name: Combat of Apeleg
events.text: c. Feb 1883: an Argentine patrol defeats a Tehuelche and Mapuche force in Chubut.

steps.label: 1884 to 1885
steps.title: Surrender of Sayhueque
steps.text: Lorenzo Vintter's columns hunted the last free bands across Neuquen and Chubut. Namuncura surrendered in 1884 and Inacayal and Foyel were captured that autumn. On 1 January 1885 Valentin Sayhueque surrendered at Junin de los Andes; survivors were deported to Martin Garcia island, forced labour or reservations, and their lands sold off.

events.name: Surrender of Sayhueque
events.text: The last great Patagonian chief lays down his arms.

name: First Sino-Japanese War
summary: Japan and Qing China fought over control of Korea after both sent troops to put down the Donghak rebellion. Japan's modernised army and navy swept the Chinese out of Korea, into Manchuria and Shandong, and destroyed the Beiyang Fleet. The Treaty of Shimonoseki ended Chinese suzerainty over Korea, gave Japan Taiwan and made it the leading power in East Asia.

steps.label: Jul 1894
steps.title: Showdown in Korea
steps.text: Both powers sent troops to Korea during the Donghak peasant rebellion and then refused to leave. Japanese troops seized the royal palace in Seoul on 23 July, and two days later Japanese cruisers sank the transport Kowshing off Pungdo. General Oshima Yoshimasa beat the Chinese at Seonghwan, and war was declared on 1 August.

events.name: Battle of Pungdo
events.text: Japanese cruisers sink a troopship and drive off its escorts.

events.name: Battle of Seonghwan
events.text: The first land battle; the Chinese fall back north.

steps.label: Sep 1894
steps.title: Pyongyang and the Yalu
steps.text: Yamagata Aritomo's First Army converged on Pyongyang and took it on 15 September, driving the Qing out of Korea. Two days later Admiral Ito Sukeyuki's fleet beat Ding Ruchang's Beiyang Fleet off the mouth of the Yalu, sinking five ships. The survivors withdrew to port and China lost control of the Yellow Sea.

events.name: Battle of Pyongyang
events.text: The Qing army is routed and flees across the Yalu.

events.name: Battle of the Yalu River
events.text: Japan wins the decisive naval battle of the war.

steps.label: Oct to Nov 1894
steps.title: Into Manchuria, Port Arthur
steps.text: The First Army crossed the Yalu at Jiuliancheng and pushed into Manchuria. Oyama Iwao's Second Army landed on the Liaodong Peninsula, took Jinzhou and Dalian and stormed the fortress of Port Arthur on 21 November, where his troops then massacred much of the town's population.

events.name: Battle of Jiuliancheng
events.text: Japan crosses the Yalu into China.

events.name: Fall of Port Arthur
events.text: China's main northern naval base falls in a day.

steps.label: Jan to Feb 1895
steps.title: Weihaiwei
steps.text: The Second Army landed on the tip of Shandong and took the land forts of Weihaiwei from behind, while torpedo boats raided the trapped Beiyang Fleet. Admiral Ding Ruchang surrendered the fleet on 12 February and took his own life. Japanese armies also advanced on Yingkou in Manchuria, and Beijing sued for peace.

events.name: Battle of Weihaiwei
events.text: The Beiyang Fleet surrenders; China has no navy left in the north.

steps.label: Apr to Oct 1895
steps.title: Shimonoseki and Taiwan
steps.text: Li Hongzhang signed the Treaty of Shimonoseki on 17 April: China recognised Korea's independence, ceded Taiwan, the Pescadores and Liaodong, and paid 200 million taels. Within days Russia, France and Germany forced Japan to hand back Liaodong. Japanese troops then fought for months to crush the short-lived Republic of Formosa.

events.name: Treaty of Shimonoseki
events.text: China cedes Taiwan and gives up its claim over Korea.

events.name: Triple Intervention
events.text: Russia, France and Germany force Japan to return Liaodong.

name: Spanish-American War
summary: The United States went to war with Spain in 1898 over Cuba, where Cubans had been fighting for independence since 1895. American fleets destroyed both Spanish squadrons, at Manila Bay and Santiago de Cuba, and US troops with Cuban and Filipino insurgents took Santiago, Puerto Rico and Manila. Spain lost the last of its American and Pacific empire and the United States became an overseas colonial power.

sides.name: United States, with Cuban and Filipino insurgents

steps.label: Feb to Apr 1898
steps.title: Remember the Maine
steps.text: Cuban rebels had fought Spanish rule since 1895, and the brutal reconcentration camps outraged US opinion. On 15 February the battleship USS Maine blew up in Havana harbour, killing 260 men. Congress declared war in April; Admiral Sampson blockaded Cuba while Admiral Cervera's squadron sailed from the Cape Verde Islands for the Caribbean.

events.name: Sinking of the USS Maine
events.text: The explosion in Havana harbour sweeps the US into war.

steps.label: May to Jun 1898
steps.title: Manila Bay
steps.text: Commodore George Dewey's Asiatic Squadron sailed from Mirs Bay near Hong Kong and on 1 May destroyed Admiral Montojo's older ships off Cavite without losing a man. Dewey brought Emilio Aguinaldo back from exile, and Filipino forces swept the Spanish from much of Luzon. Aguinaldo declared Philippine independence on 12 June.

events.name: Battle of Manila Bay
events.text: The Spanish Pacific squadron is destroyed in a morning.

events.name: Philippine Declaration of Independence
events.text: Aguinaldo proclaims the Philippines independent at Kawit.

steps.label: Jun to Jul 1898
steps.title: Santiago de Cuba
steps.text: General Shafter's V Corps landed at Daiquiri and Siboney with Cuban help and stormed El Caney and the San Juan Heights on 1 July, Theodore Roosevelt's Rough Riders among them. Trapped, Cervera's squadron ran out of the harbour on 3 July and was destroyed along the coast. Santiago surrendered on 17 July.

events.name: Battle of San Juan Hill
events.text: US troops take the heights overlooking Santiago.

events.name: Battle of Santiago de Cuba
events.text: Cervera's whole squadron is sunk or beached.

events.name: Surrender of Santiago
events.text: The Spanish garrison in eastern Cuba surrenders.

steps.label: Jul to Aug 1898
steps.title: Puerto Rico and Manila
steps.text: General Nelson Miles landed at Guanica on 25 July and advanced across Puerto Rico against light resistance. An armistice was signed on 12 August, but news had not reached Manila, where US troops under Wesley Merritt took the city the next day in a largely staged battle. Filipino forces were kept out of the city, souring relations with Aguinaldo.

events.name: Landing at Guanica
events.text: US troops land on Puerto Rico's south coast.

events.name: Battle of Manila
events.text: Manila surrenders after a token defence.

events.name: Armistice protocol
events.text: Fighting ends on 12 August.

steps.label: Dec 1898
steps.title: Treaty of Paris
steps.text: By the Treaty of Paris on 10 December, Spain gave up Cuba and ceded Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines to the United States for 20 million dollars. Cuba came under US military rule until 1902. Filipinos who had fought for independence turned on their new rulers in February 1899, starting the Philippine American War.

events.name: Treaty of Paris
events.text: Spain loses Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines.

name: Second Boer War
summary: Britain and the two Boer republics, the Transvaal and the Orange Free State, went to war over British supremacy in South Africa and the rights of foreign gold miners on the Witwatersrand. The Boers won early victories and besieged three towns, but a huge British army took both capitals in 1900. Two more years of guerrilla war ended only after scorched earth and concentration camps, and the republics became British colonies, later part of the Union of South Africa.

steps.label: Oct to Nov 1899
steps.title: Boer offensive and sieges
steps.text: The Boers struck first after their ultimatum expired on 11 October 1899. Piet Joubert's commandos invaded Natal and, after Talana Hill, bottled up the main British field force in Ladysmith. In the west, Cronje and the Free Staters laid siege to Kimberley and Mafeking, and General Buller arrived at Cape Town with an army corps.

events.name: Siege of Ladysmith
events.text: About 13,000 British troops are encircled in northern Natal.

events.name: Siege of Kimberley
events.text: The diamond town, with Cecil Rhodes inside, is cut off.

events.name: Siege of Mafeking
events.text: Baden-Powell's small garrison holds out for 217 days.

steps.label: Dec 1899
steps.title: Black Week
steps.text: Three British relief attempts failed within a week. Gatacre was beaten at Stormberg, Methuen's Highland Brigade was cut down before Koos de la Rey's trenches at Magersfontein, and Buller's frontal assault across the Tugela at Colenso collapsed. Shocked, London sent Lord Roberts with Kitchener as chief of staff.

events.name: Battle of Stormberg
events.text: A night march goes wrong and Gatacre is routed.

events.name: Battle of Magersfontein
events.text: Hidden Boer trenches shatter the Highland Brigade.

events.name: Battle of Colenso
events.text: Buller fails to cross the Tugela and loses ten guns.

steps.label: Feb to Mar 1900
steps.title: Roberts turns the tide
steps.text: Roberts swung his army east of the Boer lines: John French's cavalry relieved Kimberley and Cronje, caught in retreat, surrendered 4,000 men at Paardeberg on 27 February. In Natal, Buller was beaten again at Spion Kop but finally broke through and relieved Ladysmith on 28 February. Roberts entered Bloemfontein on 13 March.

events.name: Battle of Spion Kop
events.text: British troops seize the hilltop but are shot to pieces and withdraw.

events.name: Battle of Paardeberg
events.text: Cronje's army is surrounded and surrenders.

events.name: Relief of Ladysmith
events.text: Buller's army breaks through after 118 days.

steps.label: May to Sep 1900
steps.title: Johannesburg and Pretoria
steps.text: Roberts marched up the railway, taking Johannesburg on 31 May and Pretoria on 5 June, while a flying column relieved Mafeking. Britain annexed both republics. After Louis Botha's last pitched battle at Bergendal, the aged President Kruger left for Europe through Lourenco Marques.

events.name: Relief of Mafeking
events.text: The siege is lifted on 17 May to wild celebrations in Britain.

events.name: Fall of Pretoria
events.text: The Transvaal capital falls almost without a fight.

events.name: Battle of Bergendal
events.text: The last set-piece battle; the Boers turn to guerrilla war.

steps.title: Guerrilla war and blockhouses
steps.text: Mounted commandos under De Wet, De la Rey, Botha and Jan Smuts raided railways and columns across the veld, and Smuts rode deep into the Cape Colony. Kitchener answered with farm burning, thousands of blockhouses strung along barbed wire and drives to sweep the country. Boer families were herded into concentration camps where about 26,000 Boer women and children and at least 20,000 Black Africans died.

fronts.label: Blockhouse line along the central railway
Blockhouse line along the eastern railway

events.name: Battle of Bakenlaagte
events.text: Botha's commandos overrun a British column's rearguard.

events.name: Concentration camps
events.text: Disease and hunger in the camps cause a scandal led by Emily Hobhouse.

steps.label: May 1902
steps.title: Peace of Vereeniging
steps.text: Worn down, the Boer leaders met at Vereeniging and signed the peace in Pretoria on 31 May 1902. The republics became British colonies with a promise of self-government and money to rebuild farms. In 1910 they joined the Cape and Natal in the Union of South Africa.

events.name: Treaty of Vereeniging
events.text: The Boer republics accept British sovereignty.

name: Boxer Rebellion
summary: The Boxers, an anti-foreign and anti-Christian peasant movement in north China, killed missionaries and converts and in 1900 besieged the foreign legations in Beijing with the backing of the Qing court. An Eight-Nation Alliance of Japan, Russia, Britain, France, the United States, Germany, Italy and Austria-Hungary fought its way to Beijing and lifted the siege, while Russia overran Manchuria. The Boxer Protocol imposed a crushing indemnity and foreign garrisons, further weakening the dynasty.

steps.title: Rise of the Boxers
steps.text: In drought-stricken Shandong, the Righteous and Harmonious Fists blamed missionaries, converts and foreigners for the province's ills. After clashes with Qing troops at Senluo Temple in October 1899, Yuan Shikai crushed them in Shandong, but the bands spread into Zhili toward Beijing under the slogan Support the Qing, destroy the foreign.

polities: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

events.name: Senluo Temple clash
events.text: Boxers fight Qing troops in Pingyuan county, Shandong.

steps.label: Jun 1900
steps.title: Siege of the Legations
steps.text: Boxers poured into Beijing and Tianjin, burning churches and railway stations. Admiral Seymour's 2,000-man relief column was stopped at Langfang and driven back. After allied ships seized the Dagu Forts, the court declared war on the powers on 21 June, and Boxers and imperial troops under Dong Fuxiang laid siege to the legation quarter.

polities: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

events.name: Siege of the Legations
events.text: About 900 foreigners and 3,000 Chinese Christians hold out for 55 days.

events.name: Battle of the Dagu Forts
events.text: Allied ships take the forts guarding the river to Tianjin.

events.name: Battle of Langfang
events.text: Seymour's column is halted and forced to retreat.

steps.label: Jul 1900
steps.title: Tianjin and Manchuria
steps.text: Allied troops stormed the walled city of Tianjin on 13 to 14 July, securing a base for the march on Beijing. In the north, Boxers attacked the Russian railway in Manchuria and Qing guns shelled Blagoveshchensk, where Russian forces then drowned thousands of Chinese residents in the Amur. Russian columns invaded Manchuria from three directions.

polities: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

events.name: Battle of Tianjin
events.text: The allies take Tianjin after heavy losses.

events.name: Blagoveshchensk massacre
events.text: Russian forces drive thousands of Chinese residents into the Amur.

steps.label: Aug 1900
steps.title: Relief of Peking
steps.text: About 20,000 allied troops, half of them Japanese and Russian, marched from Tianjin on 4 August, winning at Beicang and Yangcun. They reached Beijing on 14 August and lifted the siege. Empress Dowager Cixi and the emperor fled in disguise to Xi'an, and foreign troops looted the capital.

polities: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

events.name: Battle of Yangcun
events.text: The allies break the Qing line on the road to Beijing.

events.name: Relief of the Legations
events.text: Allied troops storm the city gates and end the siege.

steps.label: 1900 to 1901
steps.title: Punitive expeditions and the Boxer Protocol
steps.text: German Field Marshal von Waldersee arrived to lead punitive expeditions across Zhili, while Russia kept its grip on Manchuria. The Boxer Protocol of 7 September 1901 forced China to pay 450 million taels, execute officials who backed the Boxers and accept foreign troops in Beijing. Russia's refusal to leave Manchuria set it on course for war with Japan.

polities: United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland

events.name: Boxer Protocol
events.text: China accepts a huge indemnity and permanent foreign garrisons.

name: Russo-Japanese War
summary: Russia and Japan fought over Manchuria and Korea after Russia refused to withdraw its troops from Manchuria. Japan struck first at Port Arthur, won a series of bloody land battles culminating at Mukden and annihilated Russia's Baltic Fleet at Tsushima. It was the first modern victory of an Asian power over a European one; Japan took control of Korea and southern Manchuria, and defeat helped spark the 1905 revolution in Russia.

steps.label: Feb 1904
steps.title: Surprise at Port Arthur
steps.text: On the night of 8 February 1904, before war was declared, Admiral Togo's destroyers torpedoed the Russian Pacific Squadron at Port Arthur. Next day Japanese ships sank two Russian vessels at Chemulpo, and General Kuroki's First Army landed in Korea and marched north to the Yalu.

events.name: Attack on Port Arthur
events.text: A surprise torpedo attack damages Russia's best battleships.

events.name: Battle of Chemulpo Bay
events.text: The cruiser Varyag and gunboat Korietz are scuttled.

steps.label: May to Aug 1904
steps.title: Yalu, Nanshan and the siege
steps.text: Kuroki forced the Yalu on 1 May, the first major land battle. General Oku's Second Army landed on the Liaodong Peninsula, stormed Nanshan and cut Port Arthur off, and General Nogi's Third Army closed the siege. When the Russian squadron tried to break out to Vladivostok on 10 August, Togo turned it back in the Battle of the Yellow Sea.

events.name: Battle of the Yalu River
events.text: Japan drives the Russians back across the river.

events.name: Battle of Nanshan
events.text: Port Arthur is cut off by land.

events.name: Battle of the Yellow Sea
events.text: The Russian breakout fails and the squadron returns to port.

steps.label: Aug to Oct 1904
steps.title: Liaoyang and the Shaho
steps.text: Field Marshal Oyama's three armies attacked General Kuropatkin's fortified positions at Liaoyang in late August. Kuroki's flanking move across the Taizi River unnerved Kuropatkin, who withdrew to Mukden. A Russian counteroffensive on the Shaho in October ended in stalemate, and both armies dug in for the winter.

events.name: Battle of Liaoyang
events.text: Kuropatkin abandons Liaoyang after costly fighting.

events.name: Battle of the Shaho
events.text: A Russian counterattack stalls; both sides entrench.

steps.label: Dec 1904 to Jan 1905
steps.title: Fall of Port Arthur
steps.text: Nogi's men took 203 Metre Hill on 5 December at enormous cost, and their heavy guns sank the fleet in the harbour. General Stessel surrendered Port Arthur on 2 January 1905. Meanwhile Russia's Baltic Fleet under Rozhestvensky was steaming around Africa, and the Bloody Sunday massacre in St Petersburg set off revolution at home.

events.name: Battle of 203 Metre Hill
events.text: The key height above the harbour falls after weeks of assaults.

events.name: Surrender of Port Arthur
events.text: Stessel hands over the fortress.

events.name: Bloody Sunday
events.text: Troops fire on marchers in St Petersburg, starting the 1905 Revolution.

steps.label: Feb to Mar 1905
steps.title: Mukden
steps.text: About 600,000 men fought along a 150 km front around Mukden, the largest battle in history up to then. Nogi's army swung around the Russian western flank and Kuropatkin retreated north to Tieling and Siping after losing some 90,000 men. Japan, near the end of its manpower and money, could not pursue.

events.name: Battle of Mukden
events.text: The last great land battle ends in a Russian retreat.

steps.label: May 1905
steps.title: Tsushima
steps.text: After a voyage of some 18,000 nautical miles, Rozhestvensky's fleet tried to slip through the Tsushima Strait to Vladivostok. On 27 to 28 May Togo crossed its path and sank or captured almost all of it, losing only three torpedo boats. Russia's naval power in the Pacific was gone.

events.name: Battle of Tsushima
events.text: The Baltic Fleet is annihilated in the decisive naval battle.

steps.label: Jul to Sep 1905
steps.title: Treaty of Portsmouth
steps.text: Japan occupied Sakhalin in July to strengthen its hand. President Theodore Roosevelt mediated peace at Portsmouth, New Hampshire, signed on 5 September. Russia ceded southern Sakhalin and its lease of Port Arthur and the South Manchuria Railway and recognised Korea as a Japanese sphere; Japan made Korea a protectorate that year and annexed it in 1910.

events.name: Treaty of Portsmouth
events.text: Russia gives up southern Sakhalin, Port Arthur and its claims in Korea.

name: Xinhai Revolution
summary: A mutiny of New Army soldiers at Wuchang in October 1911 set off a wave of provincial revolts against the Qing dynasty. Revolutionaries held the south and the Yangtze while the Beiyang Army under Yuan Shikai held the north, until a deal made Yuan president in return for the abdication of the child emperor Puyi. The revolution ended more than 2,000 years of imperial rule and founded the Republic of China.

steps.label: Apr to Sep 1911
steps.title: Guangzhou and the Railway Crisis
steps.text: Huang Xing's uprising in Guangzhou on 27 April 1911 failed, and 72 revolutionaries were buried as martyrs. That summer a plan to nationalise private railways and sell them to foreign banks set off the Railway Protection Movement in Sichuan. When troops fired on protesters in Chengdu, the court sent Hubei New Army units under Duanfang to Sichuan, thinning the garrison at Wuchang.

events.name: Huanghuagang Uprising
events.text: The Guangzhou rising is crushed within a day.

events.name: Chengdu shootings
events.text: Troops fire on railway protesters and Sichuan rises in revolt.

steps.label: Oct 1911
steps.title: Wuchang Uprising
steps.text: On 10 October, after a bomb accident exposed their plot, revolutionary soldiers of the New Army seized Wuchang and made Colonel Li Yuanhong military governor of Hubei. Hankou and Hanyang joined within days. The panicked court recalled Yuan Shikai and sent the Beiyang Army south along the Beijing to Hankou railway.

events.name: Wuchang Uprising
events.text: The New Army garrison revolts and takes the city.

steps.label: Oct to Dec 1911
steps.title: Provinces secede
steps.text: Feng Guozhang's Beiyang troops retook and burned Hankou and then Hanyang in fierce fighting with Huang Xing's volunteers. But province after province declared independence, 15 in all, from Hunan and Shaanxi to Shanghai and Guangdong. Revolutionary armies from Jiangsu and Zhejiang captured Nanjing on 2 December, and Yuan agreed to a ceasefire.

events.name: Battle of Yangxia
events.text: Qing forces retake Hankou and Hanyang but cannot cross to Wuchang.

events.name: Capture of Nanjing
events.text: The revolutionaries take the old southern capital.

steps.label: Jan 1912
steps.title: Republic proclaimed
steps.text: Sun Yat-sen returned from exile and was inaugurated in Nanjing on 1 January 1912 as provisional president of the Republic of China. Revolutionaries prepared a northern expedition while envoys bargained with Yuan Shikai in Shanghai. Outer Mongolia and Tibet used the collapse to throw off Qing rule.

events.name: Republic of China founded
events.text: Sun Yat-sen takes office as provisional president.

steps.label: Feb to Mar 1912
steps.title: Abdication
steps.text: Yuan Shikai pressed the court to give up, and on 12 February 1912 Empress Dowager Longyu issued the edict by which the six-year-old Puyi abdicated. Sun resigned in Yuan's favour, and an envoy led by Cai Yuanpei went north to escort him south, but Yuan stayed in Beijing and was sworn in there on 10 March.

events.name: Abdication of Puyi
events.text: The last emperor abdicates and the Qing dynasty ends.

name: Balkan Wars
summary: In 1912 Bulgaria, Serbia, Greece and Montenegro joined to drive the Ottoman Empire out of its last European provinces, and within weeks pushed it back to the gates of Constantinople. In 1913 the victors fell out over Macedonia: Bulgaria attacked Serbia and Greece and was beaten when Romania and the Ottomans joined in. The wars redrew the Balkans, created Albania and left grievances that fed into the First World War.

steps.label: Oct 1912
steps.title: The League strikes
steps.text: Montenegro opened the war on 8 October and its allies followed ten days later, attacking the Ottomans on every side. Bulgaria's main armies under Radko Dimitriev broke through in Thrace at Kirk Kilisse and Lule Burgas; the Serbs routed Zeki Pasha's Vardar Army at Kumanovo; and Crown Prince Constantine's Greeks forced the Sarantaporo pass.

events.name: Battle of Kumanovo
events.text: Serbia destroys the Ottoman hold on northern Macedonia.

events.name: Battle of Lule Burgas
events.text: The largest battle in Europe since 1871 sends the Ottomans reeling.

events.name: Battle of Sarantaporo
events.text: The Greeks force the pass into Macedonia.

steps.label: Nov to Dec 1912
steps.title: Salonika, Monastir and Catalca
steps.text: The Greeks entered Salonika on 8 November, a day ahead of a Bulgarian division. The Serbs took Monastir and reached the Adriatic, Montenegro besieged Scutari, and Albania proclaimed independence at Vlore. Bulgaria's assault on the Catalca lines before Constantinople failed, Adrianople held out under siege, and an armistice was signed on 3 December.

events.name: Fall of Salonika
events.text: Hasan Tahsin Pasha surrenders the city to the Greeks.

events.name: Battle of Monastir
events.text: The Serbs break the last Ottoman army in Macedonia.

events.name: First Battle of Catalca
events.text: The Ottoman lines stop the Bulgarians before Constantinople.

steps.label: Jan to May 1913
steps.title: Adrianople and the Treaty of London
steps.text: Enver Pasha seized power in Constantinople in January and the war resumed. The Greeks took Ioannina, Bulgarian and Serbian troops stormed Adrianople on 26 March, and Scutari surrendered to Montenegro in April. The Treaty of London on 30 May left the Ottomans only a strip of Thrace behind the Enos to Midia line.

events.name: Siege of Adrianople
events.text: Sukru Pasha surrenders the fortress after a five-month siege.

events.name: Battle of Bizani
events.text: The Greeks take the forts and Ioannina surrenders.

events.name: Treaty of London
events.text: The Ottomans give up almost all of Europe.

steps.label: Jun to Jul 1913
steps.title: Second Balkan War
steps.text: Unhappy with its share of Macedonia, Bulgaria attacked its Serbian and Greek allies on the night of 29 June. The Serbs held at Bregalnica and the Greeks won at Kilkis and pushed north toward Kresna. Romania invaded from the north and marched almost to Sofia, and Enver Pasha's Ottomans walked back into Adrianople.

events.name: Battle of Bregalnica
events.text: The Serbs repel the Bulgarian surprise attack.

events.name: Battle of Kilkis
events.text: The Greeks drive the Bulgarians out of southern Macedonia.

events.name: Recapture of Adrianople
events.text: Ottoman troops retake the city unopposed.

steps.label: Aug to Sep 1913
steps.title: Treaty of Bucharest
steps.text: Surrounded, Bulgaria signed the Treaty of Bucharest on 10 August. Serbia and Greece split most of Macedonia, Romania gained Southern Dobruja and Bulgaria kept only a narrow outlet to the Aegean in Western Thrace. A separate treaty in September returned Adrianople to the Ottomans.

events.name: Treaty of Bucharest
events.text: Bulgaria loses most of its gains from the first war.

events.name: Treaty of Constantinople
events.text: Bulgaria recognises Ottoman rule over Adrianople.

name: Mexican Revolution
summary: A revolt against the long dictatorship of Porfirio Diaz grew into a decade of civil wars among shifting factions: Madero's democrats, Huerta's counter-revolution, Carranza's Constitutionalists, Pancho Villa's northern army and Emiliano Zapata's peasant movement in the south. Perhaps a million people died or fled. The Constitutionalists won, writing the 1917 Constitution with its land reform and labour rights, and the Sonoran generals led by Obregon took power in 1920.

steps.label: Nov 1910 to May 1911
steps.title: Madero's revolt
steps.text: Francisco Madero, cheated in the 1910 election, called for revolt in his Plan of San Luis Potosi. Pascual Orozco and Pancho Villa raised the mountains of Chihuahua and took Ciudad Juarez in May 1911, while Emiliano Zapata's peasants rose in Morelos and took Cuautla. Porfirio Diaz resigned after 35 years in power and sailed into exile.

events.name: Battle of Ciudad Juarez
events.text: The rebels take the border city, breaking the regime's nerve.

events.name: Battle of Cuautla
events.text: Zapata's forces take the town after a week of fighting.

events.name: Treaty of Ciudad Juarez
events.text: Diaz agrees to resign and leave the country.

steps.label: 1911 to Feb 1913
steps.title: Madero falls
steps.text: Madero's slow reforms disappointed his allies: Zapata rejected him in the Plan of Ayala, and Orozco rebelled in the north before General Victoriano Huerta crushed him. In February 1913 a revolt in Mexico City became the Ten Tragic Days, during which Huerta betrayed Madero, seized power and had him murdered.

events.name: Second Battle of Rellano
events.text: Huerta's federal army defeats Orozco's rebels.

events.name: Ten Tragic Days
events.text: Huerta seizes power; Madero is murdered on 22 February.

steps.label: 1913 to Aug 1914
steps.title: Constitutionalist war
steps.text: Governor Venustiano Carranza of Coahuila refused to recognise Huerta and raised the Constitutionalist Army. Villa's Division of the North won at Torreon and smashed the federals at Zacatecas, Obregon fought down the west coast to Guadalajara, and Pablo Gonzalez took Monterrey and Tampico. US forces occupied Veracruz in April 1914, and Huerta resigned in July.

events.name: Battle of Zacatecas
events.text: Villa destroys Huerta's last major army.

events.name: US occupation of Veracruz
events.text: US Marines and sailors hold the port from April to November.

events.name: Treaties of Teoloyucan
events.text: The federal army surrenders and Obregon enters Mexico City.

steps.label: Oct to Dec 1914
steps.title: The winners split
steps.text: The Convention of Aguascalientes failed to reconcile the revolutionary chiefs. Villa and Zapata backed the Convention and occupied Mexico City in December, while Carranza withdrew to Veracruz after the Americans left. Obregon stayed loyal to Carranza.

events.name: Convention of Aguascalientes
events.text: The chiefs fail to agree and the revolution divides.

events.name: Villa and Zapata in Mexico City
events.text: The two popular leaders meet at Xochimilco and parade through the capital.

steps.label: Jan to Jul 1915
steps.title: Celaya
steps.text: Obregon retook Puebla and Mexico City and led his army into the Bajio. At Celaya in April he met Villa's famous cavalry charges with trenches, barbed wire and machine guns learned from the war in Europe, and destroyed the Division of the North. Defeats at Leon and Aguascalientes followed, and the United States recognised Carranza in October.

events.name: Battles of Celaya
events.text: Villa's army is shattered in two battles in April.

events.name: Battle of Trinidad
events.text: Obregon loses an arm but wins the war's longest battle near Leon.

steps.label: 1916 to 1917
steps.title: Columbus raid and the Constitution
steps.text: Reduced to a guerrilla band, Villa raided Columbus, New Mexico, in March 1916, and General Pershing's Punitive Expedition chased him through Chihuahua for ten months without catching him. Pablo Gonzalez burned his way through Zapata's Morelos. In February 1917 a congress at Queretaro adopted a new constitution promising land reform, labour rights and limits on the Church.

events.name: Raid on Columbus
events.text: Villa's men attack a US border town, provoking a US invasion.

events.name: Constitution of 1917
events.text: The new constitution is proclaimed at Queretaro on 5 February.

steps.label: 1919 to 1920
steps.title: Agua Prieta
steps.text: Zapata was lured into an ambush and killed at Chinameca in April 1919. When Carranza tried to impose a civilian successor in 1920, Obregon and the Sonoran generals rose under the Plan of Agua Prieta; Carranza fled the capital and was killed in the Puebla mountains. Villa made peace that July, and Obregon's election as president closed the armed revolution.

events.name: Assassination of Zapata
events.text: Zapata is shot in an ambush set by Carrancista officers.

events.name: Death of Carranza
events.text: Carranza is killed at Tlaxcalantongo while fleeing to Veracruz.

events.name: Villa surrenders at Sabinas
events.text: Villa retires to a hacienda in Durango.
